speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Good afternoon.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: My colleagues and I remain squarely focused on achieving our dual-mandate goals of maximum employment and stable prices for the benefit of the American people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Despite heightened uncertainty, the economy is still in a solid position.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The unemployment rate remains low, and the labor market is at or near maximum employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Inflation has come down a great deal but has been running somewhat above our 2 percent longer-run objective.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In support of our goals, today the Federal Open Market Committee decided to leave our policy interest rate unchanged.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The risks of higher unemployment and higher inflation appear to have risen, and we believe that the current stance of monetary policy leaves us well positioned to respond in a timely way to potential economic developments.

sentence: I will have more to say about monetary policy after briefly reviewing economic developments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Following growth of 2.5 percent last year, GDP was reported to have edged down in the first quarter, reflecting swings in net exports that were likely driven by businesses bringing in imports ahead of potential tariffs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: This unusual swing complicated GDP measurement last quarter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Private domestic final purchases, or PDFP—which excludes net exports, inventory investment, and government spending—grew at a solid 3 percent rate in the first quarter, the same as last year’s pace.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Within PDFP, growth of consumer spending moderated while investment in equipment and intangibles rebounded from weakness in the fourth quarter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Surveys of households and businesses, however, report a sharp decline in sentiment and elevated uncertainty about the economic outlook, largely reflecting trade policy concerns.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It remains to be seen how these developments might affect future spending and investment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In the labor market, conditions have remained solid.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Payroll job gains averaged 155,000 per month over the past three months.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The unemployment rate, at 4.2 percent, remains low and has stayed in a narrow range for the past year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Wage growth has continued to moderate, while still outpacing inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Overall, a wide set of indicators suggests that conditions in the labor market are broadly in balance and consistent with maximum employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The labor market is not a source of significant inflationary pressures.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Inflation has eased significantly from its highs in mid-2022 but remains somewhat elevated relative to our 2 percent longer-run goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Total PCE prices rose 2.3 percent over the 12 months ending in March; excluding the volatile food and energy categories, core PCE prices rose 2.6 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Near-term measures of inflation expectations have moved up, as reflected in both market- and survey-based measures.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Survey respondents, including consumers, businesses, and professional forecasters, point to tariffs as the driving factor.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Beyond the next year or so, however, most measures of longer-term expectations remain consistent with our 2 percent inflation goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our monetary policy actions are guided by our dual mandate to promote maximum employment and stable prices for the American people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: At today’s meeting, the Committee decided to maintain the target range for the federal funds rate at 4¼ to 4½ percent and to continue reducing the size of the balance sheet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The new Administration is in the process of implementing substantial policy changes in four distinct areas: trade, immigration, fiscal policy, and regulation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The tariff increases announced so far have been significantly larger than anticipated.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: All of these policies are still evolving, however, and their effects on the economy remain highly uncertain.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As economic conditions evolve, we’ll continue to determine the appropriate stance of monetary policy based on the incoming data, the outlook, and the balance of risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If the large increases in tariffs that have been announced are sustained, they are likely to generate a rise in inflation, a slowdown in economic growth, and an increase in unemployment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The effects on inflation could be short lived, reflecting a one-time shift in the price level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It is also possible that the inflationary effects could instead be more persistent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Avoiding that outcome will depend on the size of the tariffs’ effect—tariff effects, on how long it takes for them to pass through fully into prices, and, ultimately, on keeping longer-term inflation expectations well anchored.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our obligation is to keep longer-term inflation expectations well anchored and to prevent a one-time increase in the price level from becoming an ongoing inflation problem.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As we act to meet that obligation, we’ll balance our maximum-employment and price-stability mandates, keeping in mind that, without price stability, we cannot achieve the long periods of strong labor market conditions that benefit all Americans.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We may find ourselves in the challenging scenario in which our dual-mandate goals are in tension.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If that were to occur, we would consider how far the economy is from each goal, and the potentially different time horizons over which those respective gaps would be anticipated to close.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: For the time being, we’re well positioned to wait for greater clarity before considering any adjustments to our policy stance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: At this meeting, the Committee continued its discussions as part of our five-year review of our monetary policy framework.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We focused on inflation dynamics and the implications for our monetary policy strategy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our review includes outreach and public events involving a wide range of parties, including Fed Listens events around the country and a research conference next week.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Throughout this process, we’re open to new ideas and critical feedback, and we will take on board lessons of the last five years in determining our findings.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We intend to wrap up the review by late summer.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The Fed has been assigned two goals for monetary policy—maximum employment and stable prices.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We remain committed to supporting maximum employment, bringing inflation sustainably to our 2 percent goal, and keeping longer-term inflation expectations well anchored.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our success in delivering on these goals matters to all Americans.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We understand that our actions affect communities, families, and businesses across the country.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Everything we do is in service to our public mission.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We at the Fed will do everything we can to achieve our maximum-employment and price-stability goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Thank you.

sentence: We see—we see sentiment, their concerns that higher prices may be coming, or things like that, but—so people, they’re worried now about inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: They’re worried about, you know, a shock from the tariffs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But they really haven’t—that shock hasn’t hit yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Okay, so, you know, we’re going to be looking at not just the sentiment data, but also the real economic data as we assess what it is we should do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And remember, we’re—there will be two effects.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: One of them would be weakening economy—weakening economic activity, which translates into higher unemployment, and the other would be potentially higher inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Again, to say it again, the timing, the scope, the scale, and the persistence of those effects are very, very uncertain.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it’s not at all clear what the appropriate response for monetary policy is at this time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we’re—you know—and by the way, our policy’s in a good place, so we think we can wait and move when it is clear what the right thing to do is; really not at all clear what it is we should do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So people are feeling stress and concern, but unemployment hasn’t gone up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Job creation is fine.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Wages are in good shape.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, people are not—layoffs are—people are not getting laid off at high levels.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, initial claims for unemployment are not increasing, you know, in any kind of impressive way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So the economy itself is still, you know, in solid shape.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I don’t have anything more for you on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I’ve pretty much covered that issue.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, we don’t do a Summary of Economic Projections at every meeting, as you know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We do it every other meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so this was the meeting when we didn’t do it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I—you know, we don’t also kind of poll people, so I really—I really wouldn’t want to try to make a specific projection for where we are relative to that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We will—in six weeks, we have the June meeting, and you’ll have another SEP. I’m not going to hazard a guess here today what—as to what it would be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Again, what I would say is that we think our policy rate is in a good place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We think it leaves us well positioned to respond in a timely way to potential developments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s where we are, and that—depending on the way things play out, that could include rate hikes—sorry, rate cuts.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, it could include us holding where we are.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We just are going to need to see, you know, how things play out before we make those decisions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Well, you just captured the—this is the issue with the two goals being in tension.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s a very challenging question.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Now, there can be a case in which one goal is very far—one variable’s very far from its goal, much farther than the other.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And if so, you concentrate on that one.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, frankly, that was the case—well, it wasn’t a case where they were really in tension.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But if you go back to 2022, it was very clear that we needed to focus on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The labor market was also super tight, so it wasn’t really a tradeoff.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, if—I think you know what our—what our framework document says.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It says we’ll look at how far each goal—each variable is from its goal and also we’ll factor in the time it would take to get there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, you know, that’s going to be a—potentially, a very difficult judgment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But the data could break in a way that it’s not.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, I just don’t think we know that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The data could easily favor one or the other.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And right now, there’s no way to—no need to make a choice and no real basis for doing so.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, we don’t give Congress fiscal advice.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I—they’re going to do—we take what they do as a given, and we put it in our models and in our assessment of the economy, so I wouldn’t want to, you know, speculate on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mean, I think we do know that the debt is on an unsustainable level—on an unsustainable path—not on an unsustainable level, but an unsustainable path.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And it’s on Congress to figure out how to get us back on a sustainable path, and, you know, it’s not up to us to give them advice.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think they don’t need my advice and our advice on how to do fiscal policy any more than we need their advice on monetary policy.

sentence: [Laughter] MICHELLE SMITH.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it was quite a different situation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: What was happening last year is that over the space of six, eight, seven months, the unemployment rate went up by almost a full percentage point, and it was click, click, click, click, click each month.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, everywhere, people were talking about downside risks to the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: At the same time, payroll job numbers were getting softer and softer.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So there was a really obvious concern about downside risk to the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so at Jackson Hole and then in September, you know, we wanted to address that forthrightly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We wanted to show that we were there for the—I mean, we had been there for inflation for a couple of years, and we wanted to show also that we’re there for the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And it was important that we send that signal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Fortunately, since then, the labor market has really—and the unemployment rate have really been moving sideways at a level that is, you know, well in the range of mainstream estimates of maximum employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that concern has gotten a lot less.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, you know, you’re at 4.2 percent unemployment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think we were in a very different situation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And now we have a situation where, you know, the risks to higher inflation and higher unemployment have both gone up, as we noted in our statement, and we’ve got to monitor both of those.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We actually have a potential situation where there may be a tradeoff or tension between the two potentially.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We don’t have it yet, and we may not have it, but that’s what we [may] have, and that’s why I think it’s a very different, different situation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I can’t give you a—you know, a—I’m not going to try to give you a specific number.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I’ll just say, we’ve got—we have to now be looking at both variables and which of them is, is, you know, demanding—if one of them is demanding our focus more than the other, that would tell us what to do with policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If they’re more or less this, you know, equally distant and equally—or not distant, then we don’t have to make that assessment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, the assessment is, you wait.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I’m not going to try to be really specific about what we need to see in terms of the number.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But if—look, if we did see, you know, significant deterioration in the labor market, of course that’s one of our two variables, and we would look to be able to support that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You’d hope that it wasn’t also coming at a time when inflation was getting very bad.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, again, we’re speculating here.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We don’t know this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We don’t know any of these things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s very hypothetical.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re just going to have to wait and see how the—how it plays out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, you know, these are not talks that we’re in any way involved in, so I really can’t comment directly on them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So—but what I will say is this: You know, we had—coming out of the March meeting, we, we—the public generally had an assessment of where tariffs were going.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And then April 2 happened, and it was really substantially larger than anticipated in the forecasts that I’ve seen and in our forecast.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So—and now we—and now we have a different—we’re in a new phase where—it seems to be we’re entering a new phase where the Administration is entering into beginning talks with a number of our important trading partners.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s—that has the potential to change the picture materially or not.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so I think it’s going to be very important how that shakes out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But I—you know, we simply have to wait and see how it works out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It certainly could change the picture, and we’re mindful of not trying to make conclusive judgments about what will happen at a time when the—you know, when the facts are changing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, I don’t want to get my—we’re not—we shouldn’t be involved, even verbally, in questions about the timing of these things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Yes, we’re—of course, we follow all that data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We see the shipping data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We see all that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, ultimately, this is for the Administration to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: This is—you know, this is their mandate, not ours.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I know they’re—as you can see, they’re, again, having—beginning to have talks with many nations.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that has the potential to change the picture materially, so we’ll just have to wait and see.

sentence: And now that should actually reverse so that it’s—you know, it’s the difference between—it’s exports minus imports, so—and imports were huge, and so then it conveyed a very negative contribution to U.S. GDP—annualized GDP in the first quarter, as we all know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that could, in the second quarter, be reversed so that we have, you know, an unusually large contribution to—unusually positive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s very likely as imports drop sharply.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You could also have—you know, very likely you’ll have restatements of the—of the first quarter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL

speaker: CHAIR POWELL

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so you’ll see—you’ll see those data revised up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so I think it’s going—this whole process is going to, a little bit, make it harder to make a clean assessment of U.S. demand.

sentence: I mentioned private domestic final purchases, which doesn’t have inventories, government, or—inventories, government.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Anyway, it’s a cleaner read on private demand.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But that, that, too, probably was flattered a little bit by—you know, by strong demand for imports to be tariffed.

sentence: So that might overstate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s a really good reading, 3 percent PDFP in the first quarter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That might actually overstate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it’s not really going to—I don’t think it’s going to affect our decisions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I will just say, though, that it’s a little confusing and it’s probably less confusing to us than it would be to the general public as we try to explain this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, it’s complicated, and, you know, GDP is sending a signal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: PDFP is sending a signal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s a little bit confusing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But I think we understand what’s going, and it’s not really going to change things for us.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: No.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mean, it’s—look, the—look at the state of the economies.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The labor market is solid.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Inflation is low.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We can afford to be patient as things unfold.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There’s no real cost to our waiting at this point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Also, the sense of it—the sense of it is, we’re not sure what the right thing will be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, there should be some increase in inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There should be some increase in unemployment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Those call for different responses.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so until we know—potentially call for different responses—and so, you know, until we know more, we have the ability to wait and see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And it seems to be a pretty clear decision.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Everyone on the Committee supported waiting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so that’s why we’re waiting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, I think, going back a number of years, the link between sentiment data and consumer spending has been weak.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s not been a strong link at all.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: On the other hand, we haven’t had a move of this, you know, speed and size.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it wouldn’t be the case that we’re looking at this and just completely dismissing it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But it’s another reason to wait and see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You’re right that we had a couple of years during the pandemic where people were saying—just very downbeat surveys and going out and spending money.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that can happen, and that may happen to some degree here.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We just don’t know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: This is an outsized change in sentiment, though, and so none of us are looking at this and saying that we’re sure one way or the other.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re not.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mean, we don’t have, you know, the kind of tools that are good at dealing with supply chain problems.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We don’t have that at all.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s a—that’s a job for the Administration and for the private sector more than anything.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, what we can do with our interest rate tool is, we can support—be more or less supportive of demand.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s—that’d be a very inefficient way to try to fix supply chain problems.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, you know, we don’t see—we don’t see the inflation yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re, of course, reading the same stories and watching the same data as everybody else.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, right now, we see inflation, you know, kind of moving sideways at a fairly low level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I don’t have anything for you on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: My whole focus is on—and my colleagues’ focus is all on, you know, trying to navigate this tricky passage we’re in right now, trying to make the right decisions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, we want to make the best decisions for the people that we serve.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s what we think about day and night.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And this is a challenging situation, and that’s, that’s 100 percent of our focus right now.

sentence: I’ve never asked for a meeting with any President, and I never will.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL

speaker: CHAIR POWELL

speaker: CHAIR POWELL

speaker: CHAIR POWELL

speaker: CHAIR POWELL

sentence: You know, I think once you have a direction—a clear direction, you can make a—we can make a judgment about how fast to move and that kind of thing.

sentence: And, fortunately, as I mentioned, we have our policy in a good place, the economy’s in a good place, and it’s really appropriate, we think, for us to be patient and wait for things to unfold as we get more clarity about what we should do.
